newsitem.title: UK: How West contributed to Greek-Turkey arms buildup. [corrected 17:55 gmt]
newsitem.headline: How West contributed to Greek-Turkey arms buildup. [corrected 17:55 gmt]

text.p: By Nicholas Doughty, Diplomatic Correspondent

Western allies, spurred on by the latest crisis over Cyprus, say they are worried by the buildup of arms between Greece and Turkey and are trying to find ways of easing tension in the eastern Mediterranean.

But arms trade experts say Western countries and Russia have sold and transferred large amounts of weapons to the region in the last few years and must therefore bear some responsibility for the problems which now worry them so much.
Both Greece and Turkey, as NATO members, have received equipment from the alliance to modernise their forces, developed their defence industries and bought weapons systems outright.

Cyprus is not a NATO member. But the Greek Cypriot government, worried by the 30,000 Turkish troops which occupy the northern third of the divided island, has embarked on a vigorous programme to build up its own defences.

"The region is now in the same league as the Korean peninsula, it is one of the most heavily militarised areas in the world," said Ian Anthony of the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI).
"These countries were minor players in the arms trade during the Cold War but they have since become very important."

Tasos Kokkinides of the British American Security Information Council (BASIC) said Western countries -- particularly major arms exporters like the United States, France and Germany -- should stop fuelling the regional arms race.
"The countries that are now so upset and worried by the risks of conflict over Cyprus have been transferring thousands of pieces of heavy equipment to the area," he told Reuters.
"I think there is a danger of hypocrisy here."
The United States, France and Britain have all urged a reduction of military tension in the eastern Mediterranean.
British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind, visiting Cyprus last month (Corrects from earlier this month), said a further buildup of forces on the island "would be a big step in the wrong direction".
France said last week that the decision by Cyprus to buy Russian anti-aircraft missiles could spur a fresh arms race in a region that already had too many weapons.
Paris has sold Cyprus Exocet anti-ship missiles and more than 100 battle tanks in the last few years.

Western officials say the sales and transfer of equipment to Greece and Turkey by their NATO partners are designed to make sure all members of the 16-nation military alliance can improve the quality of their defences.
"Both Greece and Turkey had a lot of very poor quality equipment," said one official, who asked not to be identified. "We have an obligation to help them as fellow NATO members."

However, the two countries are also bitter rivals who have gone to the brink of war several times in the last decade. Tanks and other equipment designed to improve defences could also be used in an offensive, should war break out between them.

According to data published by the the International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS) and SIPRI, Greece and Turkey receive or buy more conventional weapons systems than most other countries in the world.
Both have both received hundreds of surplus tanks, artillery pieces and armoured vehicles, most of them from the United States, Germany and the Netherlands after the Cold War ended.
To comply with European arms control agreements, Athens and Ankara have had to destroy some older equipment as well -- but their forces have received a major qualitative boost.

The United States has transferred multiple rocket launchers and Apache attack helicopters to Greece, while helping to upgrade Turkey's air force and selling Ankara surface-to-surface missiles. Turkey has acquired helicopters from France and Russia, as well as British anti-aircraft missiles.
Allies have sold or given warships to Greece and Turkey.
Cyprus meanwhile is still taking delivery of some 40 Russian T-80 main battle tanks and has bought BMP armoured vehicles from Moscow for its 10,000-strong armed forces.
Diplomats say one of the major problems fuelling the arms race is that Greece is insecure about its ability to deal with any military threat from Turkey, a much larger country.
The Turkish armed forces, 639,000-strong according to the IISS, are the biggest in NATO after those of the United States -- compared with just 168,000 for Greece.
